questions.text: In a principle-fact question, the principle requires "a voluntary act done with knowledge that it is likely to cause death." The facts show the accused pushed the victim during a sudden quarrel; the victim fell, hit his head, and died. The accused did not intend to kill. An answer option states: "The accused is liable because his act caused death." Which logical fallacy does this option exploit?

options.label: A
options.text: Denying the antecedent: it assumes that because the act was not intended to kill, it cannot be voluntary.

options.label: B
options.text: Affirming the consequent: it infers the presence of the required mental element (knowledge) solely from the occurrence of death.

options.label: C
options.text: Circular reasoning: it uses the conclusion (liability) as the premise for establishing the act was voluntary.

options.label: D
options.text: False dilemma: it presents only two extremes — either full liability or no liability — ignoring partial defences.

questions.solution: Correct answer: Affirming the consequent: it infers the presence of the required mental element (knowledge) solely from the occurrence of death..

questions.text: According to the lesson, what is the critical distinction between the analytical process required for Legal Reasoning questions and that for General Knowledge questions in CLAT?

options.label: A
options.text: Legal Reasoning requires memorizing statutory provisions, while General Knowledge requires logical deduction.

options.label: B
options.text: Legal Reasoning demands a structured sequential process of isolating the rule, then the facts, then matching them, whereas General Knowledge relies on factual recall.

options.label: C
options.text: General Knowledge questions test the ability to apply principles to facts, while Legal Reasoning questions test awareness of current legal affairs.

options.label: D
options.text: Both sections follow the same analytical method, but Legal Reasoning uses longer passages.

questions.solution: Correct answer: Legal Reasoning demands a structured sequential process of isolating the rule, then the facts, then matching them, whereas General Knowledge relies on factual recall..

questions.text: A consumer purchases a sealed, branded pressure cooker from a retailer. While using it according to instructions, the cooker explodes due to a manufacturing defect, causing injury. The retailer argues the consumer failed to inspect the cooker before use. In a claim under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, which maxim is most directly applicable to establish the retailer's liability?

options.label: A
options.text: Caveat emptor — the buyer had a duty to inspect the goods before use.

options.label: B
options.text: Res ipsa loquitur — the explosion implies negligence by the manufacturer/retailer who had control.

options.label: C
options.text: Uberrima fides — the retailer failed to disclose the latent defect known to them.

options.label: D
options.text: Caveat venditor — statutory strict liability attaches to the seller for defective products.

questions.solution: Correct answer: Caveat venditor — statutory strict liability attaches to the seller for defective products..

questions.text: In criminal law, the presumption regarding mens rea for regulatory offences is best described by which statement?

options.label: A
options.text: All regulatory offences are strict liability offences by default

options.label: B
options.text: Courts presume mens rea unless the statute expressly excludes it, especially when imprisonment is prescribed

options.label: C
options.text: Specific intent must be proved for every regulatory offence

options.label: D
options.text: General intent is sufficient to convict for any strict liability offence

questions.solution: Correct answer: Courts presume mens rea unless the statute expressly excludes it, especially when imprisonment is prescribed.
